cloze.text: Oral-health role of vitamin A: forms {{c1::ameloblasts}} and {{c1::odontoblasts}}, and maintains healthy oral tissues (the {{c2::sulcus}}).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: A for Ameloblast, A in odontoblast, A for tissue health.

cloze.text: Deficiency of {{c1::vitamin A}} causes impaired night vision and {{c2::xerophthalmia}}.
cloze.extra: Xerophthalmia can lead to blindness — vitamin A is important for preventing blindness (p.300).

cloze.text: Toxicity of {{c1::vitamin A}}: headache, dry skin, hair loss, liver damage.
The vitamin B complex is essential for oral {{c1::tissue repair}}.
Deficiency of the {{c1::vitamin B complex}} causes {{c2::angular cheilitis}}, glossitis, oral ulcerations and unhealthy gingiva.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: B for Border of lips → angular cheilitis.

cloze.text: Toxicity of B-complex vitamins (from supplements): nausea and {{c1::nerve damage}}, especially from vitamin {{c2::B6}}.
Vitamin C supports wound healing by synthesizing {{c1::collagen}} (periodontium).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: C for Collagen.

cloze.text: Vitamin C deficiency (= {{c1::scurvy}}): spongy, swollen, {{c2::bleeding gums}}, impaired wound healing, loose teeth.
Toxicity of {{c1::vitamin C}}: diarrhea, stomach upset, kidney stones (rare).
Vitamin D promotes bone {{c1::density}} and is essential for {{c2::mineralization}} of teeth and bones.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: D for Delicate bones.

cloze.text: Vitamin D deficiency causes {{c1::rickets}} in children and {{c2::osteomalacia}} in adults.
cloze.extra: Both are characterized by bowed legs (p.300). WakeUpMemory: the curved part of the letter D → curved legs.

cloze.text: Toxicity of vitamin D: {{c1::hypercalcemia}} (high blood calcium) and kidney stones/damage.
Vitamin K is crucial for blood clotting: it synthesizes {{c1::prothrombin}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: K sounds like C — C for Clot. Prothrombin = PT, a blood-clotting factor (p.300).

cloze.text: Vitamin K deficiency: abnormal bleeding ({{c1::prolonged}} clotting time).
Toxicity of (synthetic) {{c1::vitamin K}}: jaundice and hemolytic anemia in infants.
Zinc speeds up {{c1::wound healing}} and tissue repair.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Zinc → Zip the wound.

cloze.text: Deficiency of {{c1::zinc}}: impaired wound healing, altered {{c2::taste/smell}}, oral ulcerations.
Zinc toxicity: nausea, vomiting, and it can cause {{c1::copper}} deficiency.
Protein helps defend, heal and repair tissues and maintains a healthy {{c1::pulp}} and {{c1::periodontium}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Protein is Pro-tissues.

cloze.text: Protein deficiency: impaired tissue repair, {{c1::enamel hypoplasia}}, poor oral wound healing.
Protein toxicity (excess): {{c1::kidney}} strain and dehydration.
Dietary fat coats the tooth surface, {{c1::raises}} oral pH and helps prevent {{c2::demineralization}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Fat Forms Film.

cloze.text: Fat deficiency impairs absorption of the {{c1::fat-soluble vitamins}}.
Excess saturated/trans fat: increased risk of {{c1::cardiovascular disease}} and weight gain.
Calcium and phosphorus promote bone density and help {{c1::calcify}} cementoblasts, ameloblasts and odontoblasts.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Calcium Calcifies Cementoblasts.

cloze.text: Calcium/phosphorus deficiency: weak bones, increased tooth decay, {{c1::delayed eruption}}, bone {{c2::resorption}}.
Toxicity: high {{c1::calcium}} → kidney stones and kidney failure; high {{c2::phosphorus}} → bone weakness and soft-tissue calcification.
1 (small) calorie raises the temperature of 1 gram of water by {{c1::1 °C}}.
The nutritional unit of 1,000 small calories is the {{c1::kilocalorie}}; food labels list {{c1::kilocalories}}.
{{c1::Malnutrition}} is the imbalance between the nutrients the body needs and the nutrients taken; it includes {{c2::overnutrition}} and undernutrition.
{{c1::Macronutrients}} make up the bulk of the diet: proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, macrominerals and {{c2::water}}.
{{c1::Micronutrients}} (vitamins and minerals) are needed only in trace amounts; they enable the body to produce {{c2::enzymes}}, hormones, etc., and their absence has severe consequences.
Adult AMDRs: {{c1::10–35}}% of calories from protein, {{c2::45–65}}% from carbohydrates, {{c3::20–35}}% from lipids.
cloze.extra: AMDR = Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range.

cloze.text: Children's AMDRs are similar to adults', but infants and younger children need more fat: {{c1::25–40}}% of calories.
Carbohydrates are organic compounds containing {{c1::carbon, hydrogen and oxygen}} (CHO); their structure dictates how {{c2::quickly}} the body uses them.
Carbohydrates are classified by the number of {{c1::sugar units}} they contain.
cloze.extra: "Mono" = one, "Di" = two, "Poly" = many.

cloze.text: Complex carbohydrates ({{c1::oligosaccharides}} and polysaccharides) break down {{c2::more slowly}} than simple sugars, giving a sustained energy release.
{{c1::Glucose}} is the most efficient energy source; all sugars convert to it.
cloze.extra: Sources: dried and fresh fruits, honey, bread, grains.

cloze.text: {{c1::Fructose}} is the sweetest sugar.
cloze.extra: Sources: fruits, vegetables, corn/maple syrup.

cloze.text: The monosaccharide {{c1::galactose}} is the milk sugar found in milk and dairy products.
Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units, at least one of which is {{c1::glucose}}.
{{c1::Sucrose}} (glucose + fructose) is table sugar / cane sugar.
{{c1::Maltose}} (glucose + glucose) is a plant sugar that ferments {{c2::alcohol}}.
{{c1::Lactose}} (glucose + galactose) is milk sugar.
{{c1::Raffinose}} (galactose + glucose + fructose) is an oligosaccharide found in beans, cabbage, broccoli and whole grains.
{{c1::Stachyose}} (2 galactose + glucose + fructose) is an oligosaccharide found in beans and soybeans.
{{c1::Fructooligosaccharides (FOS)}} are found in onions, garlic, leeks, asparagus and bananas.
{{c1::Galactooligosaccharides (GOS)}} are found in beans, lentils, chickpeas and human milk.
Oligosaccharides often act as {{c1::prebiotics}} (feed beneficial gut bacteria) and can cause {{c2::flatulence}} during digestion.
{{c1::Starch}} is the polysaccharide that stores energy in plants (rice, wheat, corn, potatoes, legumes).
{{c1::Glycogen}} is the polysaccharide for energy storage in animals; it is stored in the {{c2::liver}}.
cloze.extra: Also stored in muscles (Function section).

cloze.text: Digestion converts all disaccharides and polysaccharides into simple sugars (glucose and fructose); {{c1::fructose}} must be converted to glucose in the {{c2::liver}} before it can be used for energy.
Glucose is used as fuel by the {{c1::brain}}, nervous system and muscles.
cloze.extra: Did you know? The brain burns 20–30% of your energy and (per the book) can only use carbohydrates — a small carbohydrate dose (fruit juice, granola bar) before the exam can boost performance.

cloze.text: A small portion of glucose is stored as {{c1::glycogen}} in the liver and muscles; any excess is converted to {{c2::fat}} as an energy reserve.
Fiber (from fruits and vegetables) is not {{c1::digestible}}; it aids {{c2::peristalsis}} and the elimination of water.
Orally, fiber helps remove {{c1::food debris}} from the teeth and stimulates {{c2::saliva}} flow.
{{c1::Soluble}} fiber dissolves in water and forms a {{c2::gel-like}} substance in the digestive tract.
Soluble fiber helps moderate {{c1::blood glucose}} and lower {{c2::cholesterol}}.
cloze.extra: Sources: oats, legumes, barley, uncooked fruits and vegetables.

cloze.text: {{c1::Insoluble}} fiber does not absorb or dissolve in water and passes through the digestive tract.
cloze.extra: Source: the bran layers of cereal grains.

cloze.text: Insoluble fiber reduces the risk of {{c1::colorectal cancer}}, hemorrhoids and {{c2::constipation}}.
Higher dietary fiber intake is associated with a lower incidence of {{c1::heart disease}}.
Fiber provides {{c1::satiety}} (adds bulk and delays emptying of the stomach), increases bowel movements and regulates the body's {{c2::glucose}} absorption.
Fats (lipids) are crucial for energy {{c1::storage}}, cell {{c2::structure}} and various bodily functions.
Lipids are organic compounds composed of {{c1::CHO}} (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen).
High levels of fatty acids increase the risk of {{c1::atherosclerosis}} (plaque buildup in the artery walls) and other cardiovascular diseases.
To reduce atherosclerosis risk: limit {{c1::saturated}} fat, lower {{c2::LDL}}, and increase dietary {{c3::fiber}}.
{{c1::Saturated}} fatty acids have no double bonds ("saturated" with hydrogen) and remain {{c2::solid}} at room temperature.
cloze.extra: Sources: animal fat, palm oil.

cloze.text: {{c1::Unsaturated}} fatty acids have one or more double bonds and are {{c2::viscous}} (liquid or semi-solid) at room temperature.
cloze.extra: Sources: vegetable oil, soybean.

cloze.text: {{c1::Monounsaturated}} fatty acids have one double bond (one link has no hydrogen); source: {{c2::olive oil}}.
{{c1::Polyunsaturated}} fatty acids have two or more double bonds; they can help reduce bad cholesterol and lower the risk of heart disease and {{c2::stroke}}.
cloze.extra: Sources: fatty fish, corn oil.

cloze.text: Polyunsaturated fats include the {{c1::essential fatty acids}}, omega-3 and omega-6, which the body cannot make.
Omega-3 fatty acid = {{c1::linolenic}} acid; omega-6 fatty acid = {{c2::linoleic}} acid.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: one extra "n" for omega-3 — say "nut tree". Both have proven health benefits. Omega-3 sources: seeds, nuts, vegetable oil. Omega-6 sources: corn, soybean, vegetable oil.

cloze.text: {{c1::Hydrogenated}} fatty acids are formed by adding hydrogen to some of the double bonds in unsaturated fats; they present health risks (e.g., {{c2::margarine}}).
{{c1::Cholesterol}} is a precursor for many steroids and cell membranes, and comes from {{c2::animal}} sources only.
Cholesterol is synthesized in the {{c1::liver}}, where it is used to make {{c2::bile}} to aid fat digestion (emulsification).
{{c1::LDLs}} ("bad guys") carry cholesterol from the {{c2::liver}} to the rest of the body.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: LDL → Low (or Less) desirable.

cloze.text: {{c1::HDLs}} ("good guys") pick up cholesterol in the bloodstream and carry it back to the {{c2::liver}} to be disposed of.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: HDL → Highly desirable.

cloze.text: Lipids facilitate absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins {{c1::A, D, E and K}}.
Other lipid functions: precursor to {{c1::hormones}}; help regulate and excrete nutrients in cells; surround, protect and hold {{c2::organs}} in place.
Lipids {{c1::insulate}} the body from environmental temperature changes and preserve body heat, and give foods satiety, {{c2::flavor}} and texture.
Athletes are recommended to get {{c1::20–25}}% of total calories from fat.
cloze.extra: General adult AMDR for fat: 20–35%.

cloze.text: Proteins are organic compounds made of CHO and {{c1::nitrogen}}.
cloze.extra: Carbohydrates and lipids are CHO only.

cloze.text: {{c1::Indispensable (essential)}} amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
The 9 indispensable amino acids: {{c1::histidine}}, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, {{c2::phenylalanine}}, threonine, {{c3::tryptophan}}, and {{c4::valine}}.
{{c1::Dispensable (nonessential)}} amino acids can be synthesized by the body, but only when {{c2::nitrogen}} is present.
The 11 dispensable amino acids: alanine, arginine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, {{c1::glutamic acid}}, glutamine, {{c2::glycine}}, {{c3::proline}}, serine, and tyrosine.
{{c1::Complete}} (high-quality) proteins contain all the essential amino acids the body cannot synthesize; they come primarily from {{c2::animal}} sources.
cloze.extra: Meat, fish, poultry, eggs, cheese, milk.

cloze.text: {{c1::Incomplete}} proteins lack one or more essential amino acids; they come primarily from {{c2::plant}} sources.
cloze.extra: Nuts, legumes, grains, seeds, vegetables. They can be combined with other proteins to form complete proteins.

cloze.text: {{c1::Complementary}} proteins compensate for each other's amino-acid deficiencies when combined, e.g. {{c2::whole grains}} (rice) with {{c2::legumes}} (beans).
cloze.extra: Did you know? Because the body can't make the essential amino acids, eating complete proteins (meat) or carefully combining incomplete proteins (rice and beans) is vital for health and tissue repair.

cloze.text: Proteins assist in the growth, maintenance, construction and {{c1::repair}} of body tissues.
Proteins make hormones, {{c1::enzymes}} and {{c2::antibodies}}.
Because protein is used for both tissue repair and energy, protein requirements {{c1::increase}} as total energy intake decreases (e.g., when dieting).
When protein is used for energy, amino acids are first {{c1::deaminated}} (stripped of the amine group); the remaining carbon skeleton is used to produce {{c2::glucose}} or ketones.
The removed amine group produces {{c1::ammonia}} (toxic), which the liver converts to {{c2::urea}}, excreted in urine by the kidneys.
If protein intake exceeds needs for synthesis and energy, the amino acids are deaminated and their carbon fragments may be stored as {{c1::fat}}.
cloze.extra: In North America, protein and caloric intakes are typically well above requirements, contributing significantly to fat.

cloze.text: Dietary protein requirements increase during growth, {{c1::pregnancy}}, lactation, trauma, {{c2::surgery}} and fever.
Vegans (no eggs or milk) are at greater risk of {{c1::iron}}, calcium, protein and {{c2::vitamin B12}} deficiency, because these nutrients usually come from animal products.
Ovo-lacto vegetarians (eat eggs and milk) can get the essential amino acids but may be deficient in {{c1::iron}}.
Vitamins are {{c1::organic}} nutrients needed in small quantities; they do not provide {{c2::energy}} but facilitate many processes.
Unlike water-soluble vitamins, {{c1::fat-soluble}} vitamins are stored in the body's {{c2::liver}} and fatty tissues, so they are not easily excreted and can accumulate to toxic levels.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: a fat-soluble man relaxing on a DECK soaking up the sun: A, D, E, (c silent), K.

cloze.text: Vitamin A is also called {{c1::retinol}}; sources: {{c2::carrots}}, squash.
cloze.extra: Key functions: night vision, healthy oral mucosa and sulcus, ameloblast/odontoblast formation, preventing blindness.

cloze.text: Vitamin D is also called {{c1::calciferol}} (the "{{c2::Sunshine}} Vitamin").
Vitamin D aids {{c1::calcium}} and phosphorus absorption.
Rickets and osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency) are characterized by {{c1::bowed legs}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: curved part of the letter D → curved legs.

cloze.text: Sources of vitamin D: {{c1::sunlight}} exposure (activates a precursor) and {{c2::fortified}} milk (natural milk lacks it).
Vitamin E is also called {{c1::tocopherol}}; it functions as an {{c2::antioxidant}} (prevents vitamin oxidation).
cloze.extra: Sources: vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, green leafy vegetables, fortified cereals.

cloze.text: Vitamin E deficiency causes {{c1::hemolytic anemia}} (especially in {{c2::preterm infants}}) due to red blood cell fragility.
At high doses, vitamin {{c1::E}} can interfere with blood {{c2::coagulation}}.
Vitamin K sources: green leafy vegetables, meat, dairy; it is also synthesized by the {{c1::intestine}}.

basic.back: Substances obtained from food to promote growth, maintenance, or repair
Simple sugar: the basic unit of carbohydrate (one sugar unit)
The major form of fat stored by the body; the backbone for many types of lipids
The means of transport through the bloodstream for cholesterol, triglycerides and phospholipids
Fats the body cannot make (must come from the diet)

basic.front: What is the limiting amino acid ("limiting protein") and why does it matter?
basic.back: The essential amino acid missing or present in the smallest amount in an incomplete protein; it limits overall protein synthesis, because all amino acids must be present to build protein.
basic.extra: Varies by food source; critical in incomplete proteins.

basic.back: Meeting most energy needs with carbohydrate (and fat) saves protein for tissue repair and growth instead of being burned for energy.

typein.extra: Also called large, dietary, nutritional or food calories, or Calories with a capital C.

typein.extra: They can be arranged in different ways to make different proteins, like letters of the alphabet.

How many dispensable (nonessential) amino acids are there? (number)
How many kcal per gram does protein provide? (number)
typein.extra: Protein is used for energy when carbohydrate and fat intake are inadequate.

mcq.question: A patient with a very restricted diet presents with spongy, swollen gingiva that bleeds easily, loose teeth and slow healing of a recent extraction site. Which nutrient deficiency is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Spongy, bleeding gums, impaired wound healing and loose teeth = scurvy (vitamin C deficiency; vitamin C is needed to synthesize collagen). Vitamin K deficiency also causes bleeding, but as prolonged clotting time — not spongy gingiva and loose teeth.

mcq.question: A patient takes high-dose zinc supplements to speed healing. Which toxicity effect listed in the book can this cause?
mcq.explanation: Zinc toxicity causes nausea, vomiting and copper deficiency. Hypercalcemia is vitamin D toxicity; soft-tissue calcification is high phosphorus; jaundice is synthetic vitamin K toxicity.

mcq.question: An adult's diet supplies 1,000 kcal from fat out of a 2,000-kcal daily intake. Compared with the adult AMDR for lipids, this intake is:
options: D. Appropriate only for an athlete
mcq.explanation: 1,000/2,000 = 50% of calories from fat; the adult AMDR for lipids is 20–35%, so the intake is above the range. Athletes are advised even less: 20–25%.

mcq.question: A patient reports bloating and flatulence after eating beans, cabbage and broccoli. Which carbohydrate in these foods is most likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Raffinose is an oligosaccharide found in beans, cabbage, broccoli and whole grains; oligosaccharides feed gut bacteria (prebiotics) and can cause flatulence. Glycogen is animal storage carbohydrate, not a plant food component.

mcq.question: A patient with chronic constipation and hemorrhoids asks which food to add to her diet. Based on fiber type, which is the best choice?
mcq.explanation: Insoluble fiber (bran layers of cereal grains) passes through the digestive tract and reduces constipation and hemorrhoids. Oats and barley are soluble-fiber sources, better known for lowering cholesterol and moderating blood glucose; chicken has no fiber.

mcq.question: Which fat is solid at room temperature and should be limited to 10% or less of daily calories?
mcq.explanation: Palm oil (like animal fat) is a saturated fat: no double bonds, solid at room temperature, ≤10% of calories. Olive oil is monounsaturated; corn and soybean oils are unsaturated (polyunsaturated) and liquid.

mcq.question: A patient's lab report shows a high HDL level. How should this be interpreted?
options: A. Unfavorable — HDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the tissues
B. Favorable — HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver for disposal
C. Unfavorable — HDL is formed by hydrogenating unsaturated fats
D. Neutral — HDL only transports fat-soluble vitamins
mcq.answer: B. Favorable — HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver for disposal
mcq.explanation: HDL ("good guys", Highly desirable) picks up cholesterol in the bloodstream and returns it to the liver to be disposed of. Carrying cholesterol from the liver to the body is LDL ("bad guys").

mcq.question: A vegan patient eats rice and beans together at most meals. What principle does this combination illustrate?
mcq.explanation: Rice (whole grain) and beans (legume) are each incomplete plant proteins; combined, they compensate for each other's limiting amino acids and supply all essential amino acids — complementary proteins. Neither food alone is a complete protein.

mcq.question: Which patient has the LOWEST increase in dietary protein requirement, according to the book?
options: B. A patient recovering from surgery
D. A patient with a fever
mcq.explanation: Protein requirements increase during growth, pregnancy, lactation, trauma, surgery and fever. A healthy, weight-stable adult has none of these stresses (and North Americans typically eat well above requirements).

mcq.question: A patient takes high-dose vitamin E supplements daily. Before scaling and root planing, which concern is most relevant?
options: B. Increased bleeding from impaired coagulation
mcq.answer: B. Increased bleeding from impaired coagulation
mcq.explanation: At high doses vitamin E can interfere with blood coagulation, so expect more bleeding. Hypercalcemia is vitamin D toxicity; night blindness is vitamin A deficiency.

mcq.question: A preterm infant develops hemolytic anemia due to red blood cell fragility. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Vitamin E (tocopherol) is an antioxidant; its deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, especially in preterm infants. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired clotting (the book lists hemolytic anemia in infants only as a toxicity of synthetic vitamin K).
